planting.note: Plant fresh acorns immediately after fall collection, 1-2 inches deep, in lean, rocky, well-drained, acidic soil; maple-leaf oak is restricted in the wild to a handful of exposed sandstone and novaculite summits in the Ouachita Mountains of western Arkansas and tolerates both full sun and partial shade.

directions: Maple-leaf oak is a rare red-oak-group endemic known only from rocky summits and ridgelines of a few Ouachita Mountain peaks, chiefly Rich Mountain and Black Fork Mountain in western Arkansas, where it grows as a small, often multi-stemmed tree on thin, acidic, sandstone or novaculite soils. Its deeply five-lobed, star-shaped, glossy leaves resemble a red or sugar maple far more than a typical oak and turn red-bronze in fall, and its compact 15-30 foot stature suits smaller home landscapes as well as rock-garden-style plantings. Plant fresh acorns in fall after natural cold, moist stratification, or set out container-grown saplings in average to lean, fast-draining soil; established trees are notably drought-tolerant once past the seedling stage. Because wild populations are small and geographically isolated, source only nursery-propagated stock from native-plant specialists rather than wild-collected acorns.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto bare, lean, rocky, well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade; seedlings overwinter as a basal rosette and bloom the following spring, mimicking the open novaculite and sandstone glades of the Ouachita Mountains where this biennial grows wild.

directions: Clasping jewelflower is a biennial member of the mustard family restricted to dry, rocky novaculite and sandstone glades and open woodland margins of the Ouachita Mountains in Arkansas and Oklahoma, with a few outlying Ozark populations. It forms a flat basal rosette its first year, then sends up an erect flowering stem the second spring clothed in clasping, perfoliate, blue-green leaves and topped with the inflated, urn-shaped, maroon-and-cream mottled calyces typical of the genus. Direct sow seed onto bare, lean, rocky mineral soil in fall, since seed needs a cold season to break dormancy and the plant resents rich, amended garden soil; it suits a dedicated glade or rock-garden planting rather than a conventional perennial border. Because it is a glade specialist of conservation concern, buy only nursery- or seed-propagated stock from regional native-plant sources rather than collecting from wild populations.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall onto moist, humus-rich, circumneutral soil in partial shade, since seed needs a full winter of cold, moist conditions to break dormancy; plants form a spring rosette and take at least one full season to reach flowering size.

directions: Moore's delphinium is a little-grown woodland larkspur found in scattered, disjunct populations on rich, mesic wooded slopes over calcareous or mafic rock, including outlying stands in the Ouachita and Ozark uplifts of Arkansas and Oklahoma far west of its main southern Appalachian and Interior Low Plateau range. In mid-to-late spring it sends up slender, branched flowering stems carrying loose racemes of pale blue-white to lavender spurred flowers above deeply divided, palmately lobed basal leaves, then goes fully dormant by midsummer like many spring woodland perennials. Site it in humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil in dappled shade beneath deciduous canopy, similar to the rich-woods conditions it needs in the wild, and avoid soggy or heavy clay sites that favor crown rot. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, as with other native larkspurs, so site it away from grazing livestock and small children.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring, tucking the crown into crevices or pockets of gritty, humus-rich soil on a shaded rock face or boulder, mimicking the sandstone and novaculite bluffs of the Ouachita Mountains where this variety grows wild.

directions: Arkansas alumroot is a regional variety of hairy alumroot restricted to shaded sandstone and novaculite bluffs and rock outcrops of the Ouachita Mountains, distinguished from the widespread eastern form by its more compact habit and dense, fuzzy, rounded leaves that root directly into crevices with little soil. It produces airy, 18-24 inch spikes of small, greenish-white, bell-shaped flowers in summer that rise well above the foliage mound and attract small native bees. Because it is adapted to growing with minimal organic matter wedged into rock cracks, give it sharp drainage and avoid rich, moisture-retentive garden soil, which encourages crown rot; a shaded rock garden, retaining-wall crevice, or raised bed with a gritty mix suits it far better than a standard shade border. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant divisions in fall onto lean, rocky, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to light shade along a glade edge; this subspecies is restricted to open rocky woodland and glades of the Ozark-Ouachita Interior Highlands and resents rich, consistently moist garden beds.

directions: Ozark downy phlox is a regional subspecies of prairie phlox restricted to dry, rocky glades, barrens, and open woodland margins of the Ozark and Ouachita uplifts of Arkansas, Missouri, and Oklahoma, where it grows noticeably shorter and more compact than the widespread lowland form. In mid-spring it bears the same five-petaled, fragrant, pink-to-lavender flower clusters typical of prairie phlox, held just above downy, narrow, grayish-green foliage, and it is an excellent nectar source for early-season butterflies and native bees. Grow it in lean, fast-draining, rocky or gravelly soil in full sun to very light shade, since it is adapted to thin glade soils and will decline in rich, heavily mulched, or poorly drained beds. Division is the most reliable propagation method for maintaining the true regional ecotype, though fall-sown seed from a known Ozark-Ouachita source will also come true.
